title: How PCP Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain PCP (phencyclidine, which Chuck renders as "fencyclidine"), covering its 1926 German synthesis, its brief 1950s anesthetic use by Park Davis before its 1965 withdrawal, its rise as a street drug in the 1970s and 1980s and continued use in pockets of the US, and its pharmacology as an NMDA receptor antagonist. They discuss dissociative effects, unpredictable sedation versus agitation, the wobble weed nickname, dosing and overdose thresholds, the embalming fluid confusion, and the myth of superhuman strength and its role in police excessive-force cases such as the Rodney King trial. They also cover dependence and withdrawal, research on schizophrenia and Alzheimer's, pop-culture depictions, and a listener mail segment about manners.

segments.title: Tour promo
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck promote the remaining live tour dates in Orlando, Atlanta, and Nashville and point listeners to the tour link.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to PCP
segments.summary: The hosts introduce PCP, its full chemical name and nickname, and note that it was a precursor to ketamine and was created for legitimate uses.

segments.title: History of PCP and its decline in use
segments.summary: PCP was synthesized by German chemists in 1926 and sold by Park Davis as an anesthetic around the mid-1950s, then removed from market in 1965 due to abuse potential and side effects. Use peaked in the 1970s and 1980s and dropped sharply by 2020, though it persists in some US pockets.

segments.title: PCP in US cities and supply chain
segments.summary: The hosts discuss where PCP is still used, drawing on a Vice article, and how most US supply is linked to Los Angeles street gangs and clandestine chemists.

segments.title: Drug scheduling and anesthetic properties
segments.summary: PCP was made a controlled substance in 1978. The hosts note it shares a precursor with crystal meth and explain its sedative and anesthetic effects.

segments.title: Ketamine battlefield use and rave culture
segments.summary: The hosts compare PCP and ketamine as sedatives, noting ketamine's use as a battlefield anesthetic in Vietnam that did not drop blood pressure further, and briefly discuss 1990s rave culture.

segments.title: Brain chemistry of PCP
segments.summary: PCP is an NMDA receptor antagonist that blocks glutamate and inhibits reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, and affects opioid, nicotinic, and muscarinic receptors. It produces both depressant and excitatory effects.

segments.title: Staggering walk and wobble weed
segments.summary: The hosts describe videos of people under the influence walking with a backward lean, and explain the involuntary movements and the hippie nickname wobble weed.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before returning to the episode.

segments.title: Dissociation and sensory effects
segments.summary: PCP causes dissociation from the body, blurred ego boundaries, distorted time perception, and blackouts, and can keep someone catatonic with eyes open while still moving.

segments.title: Duration and methods of use
segments.summary: PCP acts quickly and can last about twenty-four hours. It was historically taken orally as a liquid, then smoked or snorted as a crystalline powder, and sometimes dipped into joints or cigarettes as wet drugs.

segments.title: Embalming fluid and PCP confusion
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the slang confusion between embalming fluid, sherm, and PCP, noting that embalming fluid alone is not psychoactive and that the mix-up spread through media and slang.

segments.title: Drug panic and urban legends
segments.summary: The hosts discuss 1970s and 1980s PCP urban legends and moral panic, and how the media repeated them, comparing it to crack-era hysteria.

segments.title: Superhuman strength myth and Rodney King trial
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the PCP superhuman strength myth was used to justify police force, including the Rodney King trial where officers cited suspected PCP use, and that the myth helped drive development of tasers and bear spray as less-lethal options. Chuck explains that the pain-blocking effect, not strength, explains resistance to stimuli.

segments.title: Bear spray jokes and Titanic chowder story
segments.summary: The hosts joke about bear spray and then recount a story, which they say is true, that a crew member on the Titanic film set dosed chowder with PCP, and a Bill Paxton anecdote.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break before the next section on overdose and dosing.

segments.title: Dosage and overdose thresholds
segments.summary: A normal dose is about five to ten milligrams, and symptoms can resemble schizophrenia above about ten milligrams. Dosing is hard to control when dipped in a joint, though users can control intake by taking small hits.

segments.title: PCP, schizophrenia, and research
segments.summary: PCP may worsen or induce schizophrenia-like symptoms in people with predisposition, and is used in primate research on schizophrenia and studied for possible Alzheimer's treatment links.

segments.title: Other effects: seizures, nystagmus, and personality change
segments.summary: The hosts note seizures, elevated heart rate, nystagmus, and unpredictable sedation and agitation. Chronic use can produce grandiose or spiritual beliefs and paranoia depending on set and setting.

segments.title: Addiction, dependence, and withdrawal
segments.summary: PCP has a high incidence of dependence and no straightforward pharmaceutical treatment for addiction. Withdrawal can include major depression lasting weeks and some lasting symptoms. Chlorpromazine can help reverse overdose effects.

segments.title: PCP in pop culture
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a Saturday Night Live sketch parodying PCP comedy, the 1982 film Desperate Lives starring Helen Hunt, and a Scott Baio anti-drug appearance.

segments.title: Listener mail: manners
segments.summary: Listener Amanda writes about her family's emphasis on good manners and her son Grant's listening history. The hosts discuss elbows on the table and the value of manners.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and remind them how to contact the show, followed by the iHeartRadio credit.
